sections.label: The opening
sections.line: A paywalled essay on AI burnout, and the opposite story
sections.para: Dinis wanted to read and pay for one Business Insider essay by a former lawyer who feels burned out after two years in AI, but got three paragraphs, adverts and a subscription offer, so he could not judge it. His own two years in AI were the most productive and empowered of his career: hard, but in control, with Wardley maps showing the game.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: An unbuyable essay, and two good years
sections.para: One essay, three paragraphs, then $12.95 every four weeks or $49 a year. The adverts came first, and the paywall stopped any answer. Dinis's own two years in AI were the opposite: productive, empowered, happy. Not easy, but Wardley maps show the game, and positive stories deserve telling against the anti-AI mood.

sections.label: The essay I could not read
sections.para: Business Insider's careers essay by Santiago Barraza Lopez is headlined that working in AI would put him ahead of the curve and that, two years in, he has never felt more behind. Its opening says he was a lawyer, burned out, and moved towards AI so technology would not change his profession without him. Then a subscription box covered the page.

sections.label: I wanted to pay for this one
sections.para: Dinis wanted to pay for this one essay and for its author to share in it, as with Harvard Business Review before. The page had already shown adverts in three places, earning from the visit before giving more than the headline, then asked for a plan from an organisation that has not yet earned his trust.

sections.label: I could not judge it either
sections.para: This site is building signed opinions from people who know a subject: agree, disagree, and why. With the essay none of that was possible: no way to call the headline fair or clickbait, or the story more complicated, because it could not be read. A paywall in front of an argument stops it being answered.

sections.label: Trust is earned by reading
sections.para: The newsroom's model runs the other way: five pounds of credit, a few pence per article, a price from free to double, a balance that can go negative. A publisher earns a subscription after many articles read, and can then tailor its offer, as the site tailors itself to what a reader reads.

sections.label: My two years were the opposite
sections.line: Two years of AI, the opposite of burnout
sections.para: Dinis's two years in AI have been his most productive, happy and empowered: building sgit, RiskMandate and the newsroom, combining his engineering and creative sides, shipping, scaling non-functional requirements he never could before. And his inbox is under control every day, where before it was only clean in a new job's first week or after moving everything into a folder in January.

sections.label: It is not easy
sections.para: It is not glamorous: a startup with risk and stress, failures every other week and constant blockers. Told one way it is a miserable story. Dinis sees challenges: try, step back, continue, with progress that is not linear. Corporate work is hard too; the difference is choosing what he works on.

sections.label: Seeing the game
sections.line: Wardley maps as a source of calm
sections.para: Wardley maps let Dinis see the game, the pieces, his own play and how each piece evolves, including the innovate, leverage, commoditise zigzag where each layer matures so the next can be built on it. He loves going from a half-baked idea to a release and building on it. Seeing the board turns a bad week into a move, not a verdict.

sections.label: Why tell this now
sections.line: Why the other story matters now
sections.para: There is an anti-AI mood, and burnout stories feed it. The essay is not dismissed, since burnout is real and its reasons were unreadable. But the story that this way of working can make people more productive, in control and happy should be told as loudly, especially to those starting out, which is the purpose of the Generation Z Developers book.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.para: Dinis did not read the essay and only the visible opening is quoted. Offers and adverts may differ by place and time. His experience is an account, not a study. And the anti-AI mood is his reading, not a measurement.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.para: From Dinis's voice memo of 18 October 2026 and his screenshots of the essay's page that day: headline, byline, opening paragraphs, offer and adverts.
